pages.title: What is a structure used for
pages.content:
## What is a structure used for

C programs execute from `main`. This page introduces **Structures in C** and the syntax and runtime behaviour needed to use the concept correctly.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Focus on the C language rule illustrated by What is a structure used for.

codeCard.code:
#include <stdio.h>
struct Student{char name[20];int mark;};int main(void){struct Student s={"Asha",92};printf("%s %d\n",s.name,s.mark);return 0;}

checkpoint.question: What is `ptr->age` shorthand for in C?
checkpoint.explanation: Due to operator precedence, (*ptr).age dereferences the pointer first and then accesses the member, which -> expresses cleanly.

pages.title: Unions, Memory Overlap, and Tagged Discriminators
pages.content:
### Struct vs Union: Shared Memory Model

While each member of a `struct` has its own distinct memory offset, **all members of a `union` share the exact same starting memory address**.
- **Size of Struct:** Sum of members plus padding for alignment.
- **Size of Union:** Equal to the size of its **largest member** (rounded to alignment).

```
Struct Memory:
[ int id (4B) ][ double score (8B) ] -> Total 12B (plus padding)

Union Memory:
[ int id (4B)       ]
[ double score (8B) ]                -> Total 8B (shared storage!)
```

### Tagged Unions (Discriminated Unions):
Because a union can only hold **one valid member at a time**, production C systems pair a union with an `enum tag` inside an outer struct to track which member is currently active.

callout.title: Union Overwrite
callout.text: Writing to one union member overwrites the bytes of all other members! Reading from an inactive member yields raw bit reinterpretation (type punning).

checkpoint.question: If a union contains a `char` (1B), an `int` (4B), and a `double` (8B), what is `sizeof(union)`?
checkpoint.explanation: The size of a union is dictated by its largest member, which is double (8 bytes).

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a `struct` and a `union` in C?
options: Structs can hold functions; unions cannot
In a struct, each member has separate memory; in a union, all members share the same memory space
Unions cannot be declared on the stack
questions.explanation: A struct allocates separate memory for every field, while a union overlays all fields at the same base memory address.

questions.question: Why is the `sizeof` a `struct` often larger than the sum of the sizes of its individual members?
options: Structure padding added by the compiler to satisfy CPU memory alignment requirements
questions.explanation: Hardware architectures require types to align at multiples of their size (e.g. 4-byte ints on 4-byte boundaries), leading to padding bytes.

questions.question: What does the `typedef` keyword accomplish in C?
options: Creates a new physical data type in hardware
Creates a new alias/synonym for an existing data type for cleaner syntax
questions.explanation: typedef establishes a type alias (e.g. `typedef unsigned long ulong;`), simplifying complex declarations like function pointers or structs.

questions.question: How do you access a member `val` when holding a pointer `p` to a structure?
questions.explanation: The arrow operator -> is used to dereference a struct pointer and access a member.

questions.question: What is the default integer value assigned to the first enumerator of an `enum` in C if not explicitly initialized?
questions.explanation: By default, enumeration constants start with integer value 0 and increment by 1 for each subsequent constant.

questions.question: Can a structure in C contain an instance of itself as a direct member (e.g. `struct Node { struct Node next; };`)?
options: No, because its size would be infinitely recursive (compiler error); it must contain a pointer (`struct Node *next`)
questions.explanation: A struct cannot contain an instance of itself because its size cannot be calculated. It can only contain a pointer to itself (self-referential structure).

questions.question: What compiler directive in GCC is used to prevent structure padding and pack members tightly in memory?
questions.explanation: __attribute__((packed)) instructs GCC to omit padding bytes, packing struct fields contiguously (useful in binary protocol parsing).

questions.question: Can you assign one struct variable directly to another of the same type (`s1 = s2;`)?
options: No, structs cannot be assigned with =
Yes, it performs a shallow bitwise copy of all members from s2 into s1
Only if all members are ints
questions.explanation: In C, struct assignment using = copies the complete memory layout (shallow copy) of the source struct into the destination struct.

questions.question: What are "bit-fields" in a C struct?
options: Variables that only accept binary strings
Structure members declared with explicit bit widths (e.g. `unsigned int flag : 1;`) to conserve memory
questions.explanation: Bit-fields allow packing multiple flags or sub-byte values into a single byte/word by specifying exact bit counts.

questions.question: Can a structure be passed by value into a function in C?
options: No, structs must always be passed as pointers
Yes, the entire struct is copied onto the stack frame, though passing by pointer is usually faster for large structs
questions.explanation: Structs can be passed by value in C (the whole struct is copied), but passing a const pointer (`const struct T *`) avoids copying overhead.
